summary: Describes the OSPFv2 extensions required for Segment Routing. OSPF is used to advertise the segments that nodes can use to build end-to-end paths as sequences of subpaths within the network.

plainLanguage.summary: Segment routing lets an operator spell out a path as a list of instructions, such as "go to this router, then take that link", instead of asking the network to compute one. This RFC describes how OSPF routers tell each other which instructions they can carry.

questions: what is a prefix sid in ospf
subtitle: How OSPFv2 routers advertise the labels and identifiers that let a path be built from segments.

tldr.problem: Segment Routing encodes an end-to-end path as a list of segments, but routers need a way to tell each other which segment identifiers (SIDs) they own and which label ranges they use.
tldr.mechanism: OSPFv2 carries this in new TLVs and sub-TLVs inside Opaque LSAs: router capabilities (algorithms, label ranges) in the Router Information LSA, and Prefix-SIDs and Adjacency SIDs in the Extended Prefix and Extended Link LSAs.
tldr.outcome: With these extensions OSPFv2 can program the MPLS data plane as well as the IP data plane, so SR paths need no LDP or RSVP-TE signaling. It is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted.

today: RFC 8665 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2019. The metadata for this unit records no later RFC that obsoletes or updating it. The RFC says the extensions apply to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3 where the capability TLVs are concerned, and it notes that Segment Routing can interoperate with LSPs established with RSVP or LDP.

sections.title: What Segment Routing Adds to OSPF
sections.content:
Segment Routing allows a flexible definition of end-to-end paths within IGP topologies by encoding paths as sequences of topological subpaths called segments. These segments are advertised by the link-state routing protocols, IS-IS and OSPF. Prefix segments represent an ECMP-aware shortest path to a prefix or a node, as per the state of the IGP topology. Adjacency segments represent a hop over a specific adjacency between two nodes in the IGP. A prefix segment is typically a multi-hop path, while an adjacency segment is in most cases a one-hop path.

SR's control plane can be applied to both IPv6 and MPLS data planes, and it does not require any additional signaling other than IGP extensions. The IPv6 data plane is out of the scope of this specification, since it is not applicable to OSPFv2, which only supports the IPv4 address family. When used in MPLS networks, SR paths do not require any LDP or RSVP-TE signaling, although SR can interoperate in the presence of LSPs established with RSVP or LDP. There are additional segment types, for example the Binding Segment Identifier defined in RFC 8402.

This document describes the OSPF extensions required for Segment Routing. The Segment Routing architecture is described in RFC 8402 and its use cases in RFC 7855.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of a separate signalling protocol to build a path, the routers advertise what they can do inside the routing protocol they already run, and the operator assembles the path from those pieces.

sections.title: The Identifiers Being Advertised
sections.content:
Segment Routing defines various types of Segment Identifiers: the Prefix-SID, the Adjacency SID, the LAN Adjacency SID and the Binding SID. The Extended Prefix and Extended Link Opaque Link State Advertisements defined in RFC 7684 are used for the advertisements of these SID types.

The SID/Label Sub-TLV appears in multiple TLVs or sub-TLVs defined later in the document. It is used to advertise the SID or label associated with a prefix or adjacency. It has a Type field of 1 and a Length field of 3 or 4 octets, followed by the SID/Label value. If the length is set to 3, the 20 rightmost bits represent a label; if the length is set to 4, the value represents a 32-bit SID.
sections.plainLanguage: Everything is carried in a small extra box inside the routing protocol's advertisements. The box carries either a label or an index that the receiving router turns into a label.

sections.title: What a Router Says It Can Do
sections.content:
Segment Routing requires some additional router capabilities to be advertised to other routers in the area. These are advertised in the Router Information Opaque LSA defined in RFC 7770, and the TLVs apply to both OSPFv2 and OSPFv3.

The SR-Algorithm TLV, of type 8, advertises the algorithms currently used by the router. If it is not advertised, the node is considered as not being Segment Routing capable, and if it is advertised, Algorithm 0 MUST be included. Algorithm 0 is the shortest path algorithm based on link metric, and it permits any node to overwrite the SPF path with a different path based on its local policy. Algorithm 1 is the strict shortest path algorithm, identical in the path it computes, but requiring that all nodes along the path honour the routing decision, so local policy at a node claiming support for Algorithm 1 MUST NOT alter the paths computed by Algorithm 1.

The SID/Label Range TLV, of type 9, advertises the SID/Label space of the router when prefix SIDs are given as indexes. Its Range Size is a 3-octet value that MUST be greater than 0, and the first SID or label of the range is carried in a SID/Label Sub-TLV. The TLV may appear multiple times, in which case each range is encoded in a different TLV, the originating router decides the order, the receiving router MUST follow that order when calculating a SID from an index, and the ranges MUST NOT overlap. The RFC's example shows ranges of size 100 starting at 100, 1000 and 500, which the receiving routers concatenate into the Segment Routing Global Block.

The SR Local Block TLV, of type 14, contains the range of labels the node has reserved for Local SIDs. SIDs from this block may be used for Adjacency SIDs but also by components other than OSPF, for example an application or a controller that instructs the router to allocate a specific Local SID. Each time a SID from the block is allocated, it SHOULD also be reported to all components so that they keep an up-to-date view of the allocation and do not collide.

The SRMS Preference TLV, of type 15, advertises a preference value from 0 to 255 associated with the node acting as an SR Mapping Server. For the advertisement of the SR-Algorithm TLV, the SID/Label Range TLV and the SRLB TLV, area-scoped flooding is REQUIRED, while AS-scoped flooding SHOULD be used for the SRMS Preference TLV, because mapping servers can sit in a different area from the consumers of their advertisements.
sections.plainLanguage: Each router announces which path-finding algorithms it follows and which block of labels it has set aside for itself. Other routers use that information to turn an index into the right label and to know whether a path they want is possible.

sections.title: Advertising a Range of Prefixes at Once
sections.content:
In some cases it is useful to advertise attributes for a range of prefixes. The SR Mapping Server is an example, where a single advertisement has to carry SIDs for several prefixes from a contiguous address range. The OSPF Extended Prefix Range TLV, a top-level TLV of the Extended Prefix LSA, is defined for that purpose. Multiple such TLVs may be advertised in each OSPF Extended Prefix Opaque LSA, but all prefix ranges included in a single LSA MUST have the same flooding scope.

The TLV has type 2 and carries the Prefix Length, the Address Family, the Range Size, a Flags octet, the Address Prefix and sub-TLVs. The currently supported address family is 0 for IPv4 unicast. The Range Size represents the number of prefixes covered by the advertisement and MUST NOT exceed the number of prefixes that could be satisfied by the Prefix Length without including the IPv4 multicast address range 224.0.0.0/3.

The IA-Flag marks an advertisement as of inter-area type, and an Area Border Router advertising the TLV between areas MUST set it. The bit is used to prevent redundant flooding: an ABR always prefers intra-area Prefix Range advertisements over inter-area ones, and does not consider inter-area advertisements coming from nonbackbone areas. The Address Prefix is encoded as a 32-bit value for IPv4 unicast, and the default route is a prefix of length 0.
sections.plainLanguage: Instead of one advertisement per address, a router can announce a whole block of addresses at once and give the starting SID for the block. That saves space when a controller assigns identifiers across a range.

sections.title: The Prefix-SID Sub-TLV
sections.content:
The Prefix-SID Sub-TLV is a sub-TLV of the OSPF Extended Prefix TLV and of the Extended Prefix Range TLV, has type 2 and a length of 7 or 8 octets depending on the V-Flag. It carries a Flags octet, a Reserved octet, the Multi-Topology ID, an Algorithm octet and the SID, Index or Label field.

The flags say how the rest of the sub-TLV must be read. The NP-Flag, No Penultimate Hop Popping, means the penultimate hop MUST NOT pop the Prefix-SID before delivering the packet to the node that advertised it. The M-Flag marks a SID advertised by an SR Mapping Server. The E-Flag, Explicit Null, means any upstream neighbour of the originator MUST replace the Prefix-SID with the Explicit NULL label, 0 for IPv4, before forwarding. The V-Flag says whether the Prefix-SID carries an absolute value, and the L-Flag says whether that value has local or global significance.

When the V-Flag is 0 and the L-Flag is 0, the SID/Index/Label field is a 4-octet index defining the offset in the SID/Label space advertised by the router. When the V-Flag is 1 and the L-Flag is 1, it is a 3-octet local label where the 20 rightmost bits encode the label value. All other combinations are invalid and any advertisement received with an invalid setting MUST be ignored. A router receiving a Prefix-SID whose algorithm value the remote node has not advertised MUST also ignore the sub-TLV, and if a router advertises multiple Prefix-SIDs for the same prefix, topology and algorithm, all of them MUST be ignored.

When the NP-Flag is not set, any upstream neighbour MUST pop the Prefix-SID, which is the penultimate hop-popping mechanism of the MPLS data plane, and the received E-Flag is ignored. When the NP-Flag is set and the E-Flag is clear, the neighbour MUST keep the Prefix-SID on top of the stack, which is useful when the originator needs to stitch the packet into a continuing MPLS LSP. When both flags are set, the neighbour MUST replace the Prefix-SID with an Explicit NULL label, which is useful when the originator is the final destination and wants the original EXP bits. The NP-Flag MUST be set and the E-Flag MUST be clear for Prefix-SIDs allocated to inter-area prefixes originated by an ABR and for redistributed prefixes, unless the prefix is directly attached to that router.
sections.plainLanguage: Each advertised identifier carries a set of small flags. They tell the neighbouring routers whether to strip the identifier before the last hop, whether to hand the packet on with an explicit label, and whether the number is local to this router or global.

sections.title: Adjacency Segment Identifiers
sections.content:
An Adjacency Segment Identifier represents a router adjacency in Segment Routing. The Adj-SID Sub-TLV is an optional sub-TLV of the Extended Link TLV, of type 2, with a length of 7 or 8 octets depending on the V-Flag. It carries a Flags octet, a Reserved octet, the Multi-Topology ID, a Weight used for load balancing, and the SID, Label or Index field.

The B-Flag marks an adjacency that is eligible for protection, for example by IP Fast Reroute or MPLS Fast Reroute. The V-Flag and the L-Flag work as in the Prefix-SID Sub-TLV. The G-Flag indicates that the Adj-SID refers to a group of adjacencies and may therefore be assigned to other adjacencies as well. The P-Flag indicates that the Adj-SID is persistently allocated, meaning the value remains consistent across a router restart or an interface flap. When the P-Flag is not set the Adj-SID MAY be persistent; when it is set the Adj-SID MUST be persistent.

The LAN Adj-SID Sub-TLV, of type 3 with a length of 11 or 12 octets depending on the V-Flag, advertises a SID or label for an adjacency to a router that is not the Designated Router on a broadcast, Non-Broadcast Multi-Access or hybrid network. It carries the same flags as the Adj-SID Sub-TLV, the Multi-Topology ID, a Weight, the Router ID of the neighbour for which the SID is advertised, and the SID, Label or Index field.

An SR-capable router MAY allocate an Adj-SID for each of its adjacencies and set the B-Flag when the adjacency is eligible for protection. It MAY allocate more than one Adj-SID to an adjacency, and it MAY allocate the same Adj-SID to different adjacencies.
sections.plainLanguage: A prefix identifier stands for a whole path to a destination. An adjacency identifier stands for one single link, which is what an operator uses when they want to pin the traffic onto a particular link.

sections.title: How the Extensions Are Applied
sections.content:
An OSPFv2 router that supports Segment Routing MAY advertise Prefix-SIDs for any prefix to which it is advertising reachability, for example a loopback address. A Prefix-SID can also be advertised by the SR Mapping Servers, which advertise Prefix-SIDs for remote prefixes that exist in the routing domain. Multiple Mapping Servers can advertise Prefix-SIDs for the same prefix, in which case the same Prefix-SID MUST be advertised by all of them. A Mapping Server MUST use the Extended Prefix Range TLV when advertising SIDs for prefixes, and prefixes of different route types can be combined in a single such TLV, because that TLV has no Route-Type field.

For inter-area Segment Routing, OSPFv2 MUST propagate Prefix-SID information between areas. When an ABR advertises a Type-3 Summary LSA from an intra-area prefix to all its connected areas, it also originates an Extended Prefix Opaque LSA with area-local flooding scope and a route type of inter-area. The ABR looks at its best path to the prefix in the source area, finds the advertising router associated with that best path, and uses the Prefix-SID that router advertised if it advertised one. If the router on the best path advertised no Prefix-SID, the ABR uses the Prefix-SID advertised by any other router. The same procedure applies when advertising from an inter-area route, using the best path in the backbone area.

For external prefixes, Type-5 LSAs are flooded domain wide. When an ASBR that supports SR generates Type-5 LSAs, it SHOULD also originate Extended Prefix Opaque LSAs with AS-wide flooding scope, a route type of external, and a Prefix-SID set to the SID reserved for that prefix. When a Not-So-Stubby Area ABR translates Type-7 LSAs into Type-5 LSAs, it SHOULD also advertise the Prefix-SID, using the one advertised by the router on the best path when there is one, and otherwise the one advertised by any other router. When propagating an Extended Prefix Range TLV between areas, ABRs MUST set the IA-Flag.
sections.plainLanguage: The rules say who advertises what. A router advertises identifiers for its own addresses, a mapping server advertises them for addresses it manages, and a border router passes them on to the next area, using the identifier that the best path already carries.

sections.title: Error Handling and Security Considerations
sections.content:
For any new TLVs and sub-TLVs defined in the document, if the length is invalid, the LSA in which it is advertised is considered malformed and MUST be ignored, and an error SHOULD be logged subject to rate limiting.

With the OSPFv2 Segment Routing extensions defined here, OSPFv2 will now program the MPLS data plane in addition to the IP data plane. Previously, LDP or another label distribution mechanism was required to advertise MPLS labels and program the MPLS data plane.

In general, the same types of attacks that can be carried out on the IP control plane can be carried out on the MPLS control plane, resulting in traffic being misrouted in the respective data planes, and the latter can be more difficult to detect and isolate. Existing security extensions as described in RFC 2328 and RFC 7684 apply to these Segment Routing extensions. While OSPF is under a single administrative domain, there can be deployments where potential attackers have access to one or more networks in the OSPF routing domain; in these deployments, stronger authentication mechanisms such as those specified in RFC 7474 SHOULD be used.

Implementations MUST assure that malformed TLVs and sub-TLVs defined in the document are detected and do not provide a vulnerability for attackers to crash the OSPFv2 router or routing process. Reception of malformed TLVs or sub-TLVs SHOULD be counted and logged for further analysis, and logging SHOULD be rate limited to prevent a denial of service attack from overloading the OSPF control plane.
sections.plainLanguage: Because OSPF now also steers label-switched traffic, the same attacks that could redirect IP traffic can redirect the other kind. The RFC therefore insists that malformed advertisements are rejected without crashing the router, and that the existing authentication options are used.

THE FLAGS OF A PREFIX-SID SUB-TLV

items.title: NP-Flag
items.text: No Penultimate Hop Popping: the neighbour keeps the SID on the stack.

items.title: M-Flag
items.text: The SID was advertised by an SR Mapping Server.

items.title: E-Flag
items.text: Explicit Null: the neighbour replaces the SID with the Explicit NULL label.

items.title: V-Flag
items.text: The SID carries an absolute value rather than an index.

items.title: L-Flag
items.text: The value has local significance rather than global significance.

viz.caption: THE TWO PATH ALGORITHMS DEFINED HERE

cells: The same shortest path on link metric
Any node may overwrite the path with a different one
Local policy must not alter the path

viz.caption: HOW THE SID VALUE IS READ

cells: A 4-octet index giving the offset in the router's advertised SID space
A 3-octet local label, with the 20 rightmost bits used for the label value
Invalid; the advertisement must be ignored
